29:25.ar: وَقَالَ إِنَّمَا ٱتَّخَذۡتُم مِّن دُونِ ٱللَّهِ أَوۡثَٰنࣰ ا مَّوَدَّةَ بَيۡنِكُمۡ فِي ٱلۡحَيَوٰةِ ٱلدُّنۡيَاۖ ثُمَّ يَوۡمَ ٱلۡقِيَٰمَةِ يَكۡفُرُ بَعۡضُكُم بِبَعۡضࣲ وَيَلۡعَنُ بَعۡضُكُم بَعۡضࣰ ا وَمَأۡوَىٰكُمُ ٱلنَّارُ وَمَا لَكُم مِّن نَّٰصِرِينَ
29:25.en: And [Abraham] said, "You have only taken, other than Allah, idols as [a bond of] affection among you in worldly life. Then on the Day of Resurrection you will deny one another and curse one another, and your refuge will be the Fire, and you will not have any helpers

29:26.ar: ۞فَـَٔامَنَ لَهُۥ لُوطࣱۘ وَقَالَ إِنِّي مُهَاجِرٌ إِلَىٰ رَبِّيٓۖ إِنَّهُۥ هُوَ ٱلۡعَزِيزُ ٱلۡحَكِيمُ
29:26.en: And Lot believed him. [Abraham] said, "Indeed, I will emigrate to [the service of] my Lord. Indeed, He is the Exalted in Might, the Wise

29:10.ar: وَمِنَ ٱلنَّاسِ مَن يَقُولُ ءَامَنَّا بِٱللَّهِ فَإِذَآ أُوذِيَ فِي ٱللَّهِ جَعَلَ فِتۡنَةَ ٱلنَّاسِ كَعَذَابِ ٱللَّهِۖ وَلَئِن جَآءَ نَصۡرࣱ مِّن رَّبِّكَ لَيَقُولُنَّ إِنَّا كُنَّا مَعَكُمۡۚ أَوَلَيۡسَ ٱللَّهُ بِأَعۡلَمَ بِمَا فِي صُدُورِ ٱلۡعَٰلَمِينَ
29:10.en: And of the people are some who say, "We believe in Allah," but when one [of them] is harmed for [the cause of] Allah, they consider the trial of the people as [if it were] the punishment of Allah. But if victory comes from your Lord, they say, "Indeed, We were with you." Is not Allah most knowing of what is within the breasts of all creatures

29:27.ar: وَوَهَبۡنَا لَهُۥٓ إِسۡحَٰقَ وَيَعۡقُوبَ وَجَعَلۡنَا فِي ذُرِّيَّتِهِ ٱلنُّبُوَّةَ وَٱلۡكِتَٰبَ وَءَاتَيۡنَٰهُ أَجۡرَهُۥ فِي ٱلدُّنۡيَاۖ وَإِنَّهُۥ فِي ٱلۡأٓخِرَةِ لَمِنَ ٱلصَّٰلِحِينَ
29:27.en: And We gave to Him Isaac and Jacob and placed in his descendants prophethood and scripture. And We gave him his reward in this world, and indeed, he is in the Hereafter among the righteous

4:164.ar: وَرُسُلࣰ ا قَدۡ قَصَصۡنَٰهُمۡ عَلَيۡكَ مِن قَبۡلُ وَرُسُلࣰ ا لَّمۡ نَقۡصُصۡهُمۡ عَلَيۡكَۚ وَكَلَّمَ ٱللَّهُ مُوسَىٰ تَكۡلِيمࣰ ا
4:164.en: And [We sent] messengers about whom We have related [their stories] to you before and messengers about whom We have not related to you. And Allah spoke to Moses with [direct] speech

40:60.ar: وَقَالَ رَبُّكُمُ ٱدۡعُونِيٓ أَسۡتَجِبۡ لَكُمۡۚ إِنَّ ٱلَّذِينَ يَسۡتَكۡبِرُونَ عَنۡ عِبَادَتِي سَيَدۡخُلُونَ جَهَنَّمَ دَاخِرِينَ
40:60.en: And your Lord says, "Call upon Me; I will respond to you." Indeed, those who disdain My worship will enter Hell [rendered] contemptible

3:154.ar: ثُمَّ أَنزَلَ عَلَيۡكُم مِّنۢ بَعۡدِ ٱلۡغَمِّ أَمَنَةࣰ نُّعَاسࣰ ا يَغۡشَىٰ طَآئِفَةࣰ مِّنكُمۡۖ وَطَآئِفَةࣱ قَدۡ أَهَمَّتۡهُمۡ أَنفُسُهُمۡ يَظُنُّونَ بِٱللَّهِ غَيۡرَ ٱلۡحَقِّ ظَنَّ ٱلۡجَٰهِلِيَّةِۖ يَقُولُونَ هَل لَّنَا مِنَ ٱلۡأَمۡرِ مِن شَيۡءࣲۗ قُلۡ إِنَّ ٱلۡأَمۡرَ كُلَّهُۥ لِلَّهِۗ يُخۡفُونَ فِيٓ أَنفُسِهِم مَّا لَا يُبۡدُونَ لَكَۖ يَقُولُونَ لَوۡ كَانَ لَنَا مِنَ ٱلۡأَمۡرِ شَيۡءࣱ مَّا قُتِلۡنَا هَٰهُنَاۗ قُل لَّوۡ كُنتُمۡ فِي بُيُوتِكُمۡ لَبَرَزَ ٱلَّذِينَ كُتِبَ عَلَيۡهِمُ ٱلۡقَتۡلُ إِلَىٰ مَضَاجِعِهِمۡۖ وَلِيَبۡتَلِيَ ٱللَّهُ مَا فِي صُدُورِكُمۡ وَلِيُمَحِّصَ مَا فِي قُلُوبِكُمۡۚ وَٱللَّهُ عَلِيمُۢ بِذَاتِ ٱلصُّدُورِ
3:154.en: Then after distress, He sent down upon you security [in the form of] drowsiness, overcoming a faction of you, while another faction worried about themselves, thinking of Allah other than the truth - the thought of ignorance, saying, "Is there anything for us [to have done] in this matter?" Say, "Indeed, the matter belongs completely to Allah." They conceal within themselves what they will not reveal to you. They say, "If there was anything we could have done in the matter, some of us would not have been killed right here." Say, "Even if you had been inside your houses, those decreed to be killed would have come out to their death beds." [It was] so that Allah might test what is in your breasts and purify what is in your hearts. And Allah is Knowing of that within the breasts

12:87.ar: يَٰبَنِيَّ ٱذۡهَبُواْ فَتَحَسَّسُواْ مِن يُوسُفَ وَأَخِيهِ وَلَا تَاْيۡـَٔسُواْ مِن رَّوۡحِ ٱللَّهِۖ إِنَّهُۥ لَا يَاْيۡـَٔسُ مِن رَّوۡحِ ٱللَّهِ إِلَّا ٱلۡقَوۡمُ ٱلۡكَٰفِرُونَ
12:87.en: O my sons, go and find out about Joseph and his brother and despair not of relief from Allah. Indeed, no one despairs of relief from Allah except the disbelieving people

15:56.ar: قَالَ وَمَن يَقۡنَطُ مِن رَّحۡمَةِ رَبِّهِۦٓ إِلَّا ٱلضَّآلُّونَ
15:56.en: He said, "And who despairs of the mercy of his Lord except for those astray

93:3.en: Your Lord has not taken leave of you, [O Muhammad], nor has He detested [you]

21:68.ar: قَالُواْ حَرِّقُوهُ وَٱنصُرُوٓاْ ءَالِهَتَكُمۡ إِن كُنتُمۡ فَٰعِلِينَ
21:68.en: They said, "Burn him and support your gods - if you are to act

21:69.ar: قُلۡنَا يَٰنَارُ كُونِي بَرۡدࣰ ا وَسَلَٰمًا عَلَىٰٓ إِبۡرَٰهِيمَ
21:69.en: Allah said, "O fire, be coolness and safety upon Abraham

21:70.ar: وَأَرَادُواْ بِهِۦ كَيۡدࣰ ا فَجَعَلۡنَٰهُمُ ٱلۡأَخۡسَرِينَ
21:70.en: And they intended for him harm, but We made them the greatest losers

31:25.ar: وَلَئِن سَأَلۡتَهُم مَّنۡ خَلَقَ ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَٱلۡأَرۡضَ لَيَقُولُنَّ ٱللَّهُۚ قُلِ ٱلۡحَمۡدُ لِلَّهِۚ بَلۡ أَكۡثَرُهُمۡ لَا يَعۡلَمُونَ
31:25.en: And if you asked them, "Who created the heavens and earth?" they would surely say, "Allah." Say, "[All] praise is [due] to Allah "; but most of them do not know

43:9.ar: وَلَئِن سَأَلۡتَهُم مَّنۡ خَلَقَ ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَٱلۡأَرۡضَ لَيَقُولُنَّ خَلَقَهُنَّ ٱلۡعَزِيزُ ٱلۡعَلِيمُ
43:9.en: And if you should ask them, "Who has created the heavens and the earth?" they would surely say, "They were created by the Exalted in Might, the Knowing

9:31.ar: ٱتَّخَذُوٓاْ أَحۡبَارَهُمۡ وَرُهۡبَٰنَهُمۡ أَرۡبَابࣰ ا مِّن دُونِ ٱللَّهِ وَٱلۡمَسِيحَ ٱبۡنَ مَرۡيَمَ وَمَآ أُمِرُوٓاْ إِلَّا لِيَعۡبُدُوٓاْ إِلَٰهࣰ ا وَٰحِدࣰ اۖ لَّآ إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا هُوَۚ سُبۡحَٰنَهُۥ عَمَّا يُشۡرِكُونَ
9:31.en: They have taken their scholars and monks as lords besides Allah, and [also] the Messiah, the son of Mary. And they were not commanded except to worship one God; there is no deity except Him. Exalted is He above whatever they associate with Him

9:34.ar: ۞يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوٓاْ إِنَّ كَثِيرࣰ ا مِّنَ ٱلۡأَحۡبَارِ وَٱلرُّهۡبَانِ لَيَأۡكُلُونَ أَمۡوَٰلَ ٱلنَّاسِ بِٱلۡبَٰطِلِ وَيَصُدُّونَ عَن سَبِيلِ ٱللَّهِۗ وَٱلَّذِينَ يَكۡنِزُونَ ٱلذَّهَبَ وَٱلۡفِضَّةَ وَلَا يُنفِقُونَهَا فِي سَبِيلِ ٱللَّهِ فَبَشِّرۡهُم بِعَذَابٍ أَلِيمࣲ‏
9:34.en: O you who have believed, indeed many of the scholars and the monks devour the wealth of people unjustly and avert [them] from the way of Allah. And those who hoard gold and silver and spend it not in the way of Allah - give them tidings of a painful punishment

9:35.ar: يَوۡمَ يُحۡمَىٰ عَلَيۡهَا فِي نَارِ جَهَنَّمَ فَتُكۡوَىٰ بِهَا جِبَاهُهُمۡ وَجُنُوبُهُمۡ وَظُهُورُهُمۡۖ هَٰذَا مَا كَنَزۡتُمۡ لِأَنفُسِكُمۡ فَذُوقُواْ مَا كُنتُمۡ تَكۡنِزُونَ
9:35.en: The Day when it will be heated in the fire of Hell and seared therewith will be their foreheads, their flanks, and their backs, [it will be said], "This is what you hoarded for yourselves, so taste what you used to hoard

16:123.ar: ثُمَّ أَوۡحَيۡنَآ إِلَيۡكَ أَنِ ٱتَّبِعۡ مِلَّةَ إِبۡرَٰهِيمَ حَنِيفࣰ اۖ وَمَا كَانَ مِنَ ٱلۡمُشۡرِكِينَ
16:123.en: Then We revealed to you, [O Muhammad], to follow the religion of Abraham, inclining toward truth; and he was not of those who associate with Allah

6:74.ar: ۞وَإِذۡ قَالَ إِبۡرَٰهِيمُ لِأَبِيهِ ءَازَرَ أَتَتَّخِذُ أَصۡنَامًا ءَالِهَةً إِنِّيٓ أَرَىٰكَ وَقَوۡمَكَ فِي ضَلَٰلࣲ مُّبِينࣲ‏
6:74.en: And [mention, O Muhammad], when Abraham said to his father Azar, "Do you take idols as deities? Indeed, I see you and your people to be in manifest error

28:85.ar: إِنَّ ٱلَّذِي فَرَضَ عَلَيۡكَ ٱلۡقُرۡءَانَ لَرَآدُّكَ إِلَىٰ مَعَادࣲۚ قُل رَّبِّيٓ أَعۡلَمُ مَن جَآءَ بِٱلۡهُدَىٰ وَمَنۡ هُوَ فِي ضَلَٰلࣲ مُّبِينࣲ‏
28:85.en: Indeed, [O Muhammad], He who imposed upon you the Qur'an will take you back to a place of return. Say, "My Lord is most knowing of who brings guidance and who is in clear error

0exb9O3AGHs.title: Surah Al-Ankabut: The Problem of Pain, Despair of Mercy, and Ibrahim's Emigration (29:18-26)
0exb9O3AGHs.one_line: Understanding the harsh nature of life protects faith from the problem of pain; Ibrahim exposes idols as a business and emigrates to his Lord.
0exb9O3AGHs.summary: He explains that the Quran names only enough prophets to cover the variety of human experience, and that trials of ease can be harder than trials of hardship. The parenthetical verses telling people to travel and see how creation began answer a common reason people abandon faith: pain. Those who lose faith over suffering were promised a gentle world that never existed; desert life, short lifespans, child deaths and the Mongol sack of Baghdad show that hardship is the normal texture of history, so even the horrors in Gaza, grave as they are, should not shake one's faith. Whoever objects to creation has never created anything. Grasping how much we already received should make us shy to demand more of this world, though dua remains commanded. Disbelief in Allah's signs and the meeting with Him leads to despair of His mercy, which is a consequence of false beliefs; describing the ummah's dire state honestly is not despair but the first step out of it, unlike preachers who please crowds with flattering words. Ibrahim's people answered his arguments with fire; he then showed that idols were a bond of shared interest, as Quraysh's idols secured their trade routes, a pattern repeated by shrine and faith-healing industries. Only Lut believed, and Ibrahim emigrated to his Lord, preparing the Prophet for his own Hijrah.

outline.heading: Prophets mentioned only as much as we need
outline.gist: Many prophets are unnamed because human experiences overlap; the Quran gives enough variety without repetition.

outline.heading: Prophets chosen for the variety of their trials
outline.gist: Some prophets contemporary with those named are omitted; those mentioned each had a distinctive experience to learn from.

outline.heading: The trial of ease can be harder than hardship
outline.gist: Hardship mainly demands patience, while wealth and openings bring complex duties where people hold back or spend wrongly.

outline.heading: Recap: Nuh's length and Ibrahim's arguments
outline.gist: Ibrahim's story is longer here because we hear his full address to his people.

outline.heading: The parenthetical verses: travel and see how creation began
outline.gist: Your relationship with life cannot be right unless you understand its origin, nature and laws.

outline.heading: The problem of pain
outline.gist: Many religious people leave faith because of suffering; the objection comes from ignorance of the nature of this world.

outline.heading: Life in the desert: what the Arabs knew
outline.gist: Countless people vanished in the desert; average lifespan was under forty and most infants died in their first two years.

outline.heading: The student robbed after Jumuah
outline.gist: He prayed, gave charity and was mugged, and asked why; faith is not a contract for an easy life.

outline.heading: Who are you to object to creation?
outline.gist: No one who has never created from nothing can propose a painless creation; we come from a harsh nature and live in it for a time.

outline.heading: Shy to ask for more of this world
outline.gist: Someone who grasped how much he was given unearned would hesitate to demand more, though dua is commanded and abandoning it is warned against.

outline.heading: Selling faith when harmed; questions about Gaza
outline.gist: Those who equate people's harm with Allah's punishment trade away faith; people send him questions doubting Allah over Gaza.

outline.heading: History is full of such horrors
outline.gist: The Mongols in Baghdad killed beyond counting; the tragedy is grave and will be asked about, but losing faith over it shows ignorance of history.

outline.heading: "You cannot escape, on earth or in the heavens"
outline.gist: Ibrahim's words reach beyond his age: even flying to the moon one cannot evade Allah.

outline.heading: Wali and nasir
outline.gist: A wali stands by you permanently with support; a nasir comes to your aid when needed.

outline.heading: "Despaired of My mercy": Allah takes over the speech
outline.gist: The address shifts from Ibrahim's voice to Allah's own, a classical Arabic device to hold the listener.

outline.heading: Everyday signs we stop noticing
outline.gist: The signs meant are those around us daily; habit dulls wonder, as locals ignore a famous waterfall, and knowledge of the cell restores awe.

outline.heading: A hundred mercies
outline.gist: Allah sent one mercy to earth by which creatures care for their young and kept ninety-nine for the Day of Judgment.

outline.heading: Even Iblis will crane his neck
outline.gist: A report, weak to some, says the mercy will be so vast that Iblis hopes for it; those who denied the meeting will have despaired.

outline.heading: Despair as the fruit of false beliefs
outline.gist: Some commentators say despair is not a penalty but where a corrupt understanding leads; only the misguided despair of Allah's mercy.

outline.heading: "No harm, a purification"
outline.gist: The old man who answered the Prophet's comfort by insisting the fever would kill him got what he chose.

outline.heading: Describing reality is not despair
outline.gist: We are commanded to reflect, review and correct, not to despair; the ummah cannot leave the bottom without admitting it is there.

outline.heading: The state of the ummah
outline.gist: Political, economic, social and environmental corruption, and Muslims absorbed in worldly pleasure and fear of death.

outline.heading: "He pleased us with words, so we pleased him with words"
outline.gist: A king rewarded a flattering poet with promises only; preachers who tell crowds they are blameless win audiences but lie to them.

outline.heading: Hope lasts as long as work lasts
outline.gist: We never despair of Allah's help, but must describe our condition accurately to rise from it.

outline.heading: Recitation: "Kill him or burn him"
outline.gist: Recitation of the passage on Ibrahim's people's answer, the fire, the idols and his emigration.

outline.heading: Arguments answered with violence; no two stories identical
outline.gist: His people had no answer but murder; every Quranic retelling, including Musa's, differs in purpose and detail.

outline.heading: Saved from the fire and expelled
outline.gist: Thrown by catapult into a towering fire, he walked out unharmed; Nimrod could not kill him and ordered him out.

outline.heading: Idols as a bond of shared interest; tawhid is innate
outline.gist: Most scientists accept some originator of the universe; true atheists are few, so idol worship was never about belief.

outline.heading: Quraysh's idols secured their trade
outline.gist: Each tribe on the caravan routes kept its idol at the Ka'bah, which bought safe passage; Quraysh feared starvation without them.

outline.heading: It always comes back to money
outline.gist: Removing a tribe's idol humiliated it; idols promised healing, sons and protection from envy in return for offerings.

outline.heading: They will disown and curse each other
outline.gist: On Judgment Day the partners in these arrangements turn on one another, and all end in the Fire.

outline.heading: Control through fear of the unseen
outline.gist: Faith-healing tents, shrines of saints and offerings at trees use fear of the unseen to take people's money and minds, as the Quran says of priests.

outline.heading: Follow the creed of Ibrahim
outline.gist: World powers agree at the top while the poor are bombed; Ibrahim's insight is why the Prophet was told to follow his creed.

outline.heading: Lut believed in him; who was Azar?
outline.gist: Lut was his nephew; scholars such as ar-Razi held Azar was his uncle; Lut accepted Ibrahim's message, beyond believing in Allah.

outline.heading: "I am emigrating to my Lord": preparing the Hijrah
outline.gist: Revealed just before the Prophet's Hijrah, it shows him that Ibrahim left with only Lut, while he would leave with many companions.

outline.heading: Emigrating to where you can worship freely
outline.gist: Leave a land where you are forced away from faith for one where you can worship and speak about Allah openly.

outline.heading: Interlude
After prayer: the narrator Zayd ibn Thabit
outline.gist: Beginning a reminder on a hadith from Bukhari and Muslim, he notes Zayd ibn Thabit's exceptional memory and his role as a hafiz and compiler of the Quran.

themes.label: Trials, hardship and resilience
themes.note: Pain is part of the nature of this world; understanding that prevents trials from destroying faith.

themes.label: Atheism, doubt and responding to disbelief
themes.note: The problem of pain arises from false expectations about life; no one who cannot create may object to creation.

themes.label: Palestine, Gaza and the suffering of Muslims
themes.note: Gaza is grave and will be accounted for, but must not become a reason to doubt Allah.

themes.label: Hope, fear and the balance between them
themes.note: Despair of Allah's mercy comes from false beliefs; hope remains while work remains.

themes.label: Truthfulness and honesty
themes.note: Describing the ummah's condition honestly is necessary; flattering audiences is lying to them.

themes.label: Tawhid and worship of Allah alone
themes.note: Idols were sustained by material interests and fear of the unseen, not by conviction.

themes.label: Wealth, asceticism (zuhd), consumerism and money
themes.note: Most human problems, including idolatry in Makkah, trace back to money.

themes.label: Stories of earlier prophets
themes.note: Ibrahim survives the fire, exposes idolatry and emigrates with Lut.

VzQ6tfmNxbQ.speaker_note: his Friday Arabic tafsir circle, continuing Surat Al-Ankabut from where he stopped the previous week
VzQ6tfmNxbQ.title: Friday Arabic Tafsir: Surat Al-Ankabut 25-30
VzQ6tfmNxbQ.one_line: Ibrahim reads his expulsion as hijrah to his Lord, how to read trials well, and Lut's people who turned indecency into the public norm.
VzQ6tfmNxbQ.summary: He reminds the audience that Al-Ankabut is about people's relationship with the time they live in and its trials: trials are promised like death, so running from them wastes life, and the only sensible course is to prepare, accept and handle them well. Each prophet in the passage had a distinct trial: Nuh the length of his mission, Ibrahim few followers, endless argument and exile. Ibrahim's words 'I am emigrating to my Lord' show him reading his expulsion as an opening from Allah rather than a defeat. From this he builds a lesson on reading what happens to us: every loss can be read many ways, and the believer chooses the reading that matches a good opinion of Allah, which is truth, not self-deception. He uses Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, folk tales of 'perhaps it is good', and the fifty years between Ibrahim's hijrah and the gift of Ishaq and Ya'qub. Turning to Lut, he explains fahisha, argues that 'cutting the way' means destroying family life, and that Lut's people were destroyed because they normalised indecency in public. He applies this to Western society, urging Muslims to keep calling wrong what it is, protect children and modesty, and make marriage easy.

outline.heading: Al-Ankabut: people and the age they live in
outline.gist: The surah addresses the great puzzle of what happens to people in their short life; scientific progress has not removed fear of an unknown future.

outline.heading: Trials are promised, like death
outline.gist: You will be tested as surely as you will die; fleeing what you must meet wastes time, so prepare for it instead.

outline.heading: Accepting death makes self-reform possible
outline.gist: A soul that expects a long life postpones change; one who sees death near can discipline itself, and life's trials come whether you want them or not.

outline.heading: Each prophet's distinct trial: Nuh and Ibrahim
outline.gist: Nuh was tested by the length of his mission, Ibrahim by few followers in his lifetime and opponents deaf to reason.

outline.heading: Why Ibrahim's story is told this way here
outline.gist: Quranic stories never repeat for repetition's sake; here the burning and the debate over idols are compressed so we see his patience and suffering.

outline.heading: Each story's details serve its surah: Musa in Al-Qasas
outline.gist: Details of Musa's mother, the fight and Madyan appear only in Al-Qasas because they fit its axis; even the word choice is precise.

outline.heading: Idols as a bond of convenience; only Lut believed
outline.gist: Their idols were an agreement over money and power that will turn to mutual cursing on the Day; Lut, his nephew, was the one who believed.

outline.heading: Revealed before the Prophet's hijrah; being driven from one's people
outline.gist: The passage prepared the Prophet for leaving Makkah; everyone in the room has left their own people and knows that grief.

outline.heading: 'Emigrating to my Lord': Ibrahim's journeys
outline.gist: He moved from Iraq to Sham, Palestine, Egypt and Makkah because no people received him, yet he named it hijrah to Allah, not banishment.

outline.heading: Hijrah of the body and of the soul
outline.gist: The Prophet defined the emigrant as one who leaves what Allah forbade; our calendar is tied to the hijrah, and one who cannot move can still emigrate from sin.

outline.heading: Choosing how to read a trial
outline.gist: Ibrahim could have seen only burning and expulsion; every illness, failure or injustice can be read many ways, and we pick the reading.

outline.heading: Prison as seclusion, exile as travel, death as martyrdom
outline.gist: An early saying of uncertain attribution shows how a believer can see what enemies do to him.

outline.heading: Islam never asks you to lie to yourself
outline.gist: Good readings are truth, not comforting fictions; humility is simply the fact that you are no better than any creature.

outline.heading: Losing a job: reading the situation badly
outline.gist: Seek your right from an oppressor, but seeing dismissal as the end of your life is a failure to read it; restricted provision is not Allah's contempt.

outline.heading: Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas accepts his blindness
outline.gist: Though his prayers were answered, he would not pray for his sight: a matter Allah chose for him, he chose for himself.

outline.heading: The Mighty, the Wise: what hurt you made you
outline.gist: Without the hijrah there would be no Hajar and no Ismail; the past you regret produced who you are today.

outline.heading: 'Perhaps it is good': the king and his minister
outline.gist: A minister who said 'perhaps it is good' about the king's cut finger, and about his own death sentence, was proven right when cannibals spared the wounded king.

outline.heading: The farmer's horse: 'Allah knows'
outline.gist: A new horse, a son's broken leg, and escape from conscription show that no one knows where good lies; your reading follows your opinion of Allah.

outline.heading: The Prophet loved Makkah yet saw his hijrah as good
outline.gist: Makkah remained the land he loved most, yet he did not read leaving it as evil.

outline.heading: Ishaq and Ya'qub: an answer fifty years later
outline.gist: Allah joins Ibrahim's hijrah and the gift of Ishaq and Ya'qub though decades separate them; humans are made of haste and want everything now.

outline.heading: Glorify Allah at the moment of trial, not fifty years on
outline.gist: You need not wait to see the good with your own eyes; understand about Allah beforehand, be patient and look for the positive side.

outline.heading: Prophethood and scripture in his line; reward in this world
outline.gist: From Ismail came Muhammad and from Ishaq the prophets of Bani Isra'il; Ibrahim saw things settle only late in life.

outline.heading: What comes easily is not valued
outline.gist: Children given everything rarely appreciate it; parents withhold to teach, so why resent Allah withholding to discipline us?

outline.heading: Recitation of Lut's passage and reading i'tina
outline.gist: He recites the verses and explains why the connecting hamza of i'tina becomes ya when one starts from it, a common test for ijazah students.

outline.heading: Lut sent to Sodom as a stranger
outline.gist: Sent to the Dead Sea region and not one of its people, he faced the harder acceptance any outsider calling for reform faces.

outline.heading: What fahisha means
outline.gist: In the Shariah fahisha names sins that violate modesty and honour, unlike shirk; even its whispered letters suggest something that spreads.

outline.heading: No common ground with the West on this
outline.gist: The Quran separates fawahish from sin, transgression and shirk; Muslims share much with others on freedoms and rights, but not here.

outline.heading: Their crime: making the wrong normal
outline.gist: Sin exists in every society; Lut's people were the first to declare it acceptable, which is what casual relations outside marriage now are.

outline.heading: 'Cutting the way': destroying family life
outline.gist: Against most commentators who read highway robbery, he understands it as cutting off marriage, children and the household.

outline.heading: Committing it in your gatherings: public normalisation
outline.gist: A nadi is the public space; a sin hidden behind doors differs from one carried openly into common life, like bringing beer into the masjid.

outline.heading: Not the devil's helpers, but no relabelling
outline.gist: We support a sinning brother and never despise him, yet teach our children that what school treats as normal remains wrong, even if few walk the path.

outline.heading: Those who flaunt sin, and children's books
outline.gist: Private struggles are not to be imposed on community gatherings; all the ummah is pardoned except those who flaunt, and books for small children now present two fathers.

outline.heading: Children, sexuality and the phone
outline.gist: Children cannot grasp these matters; five minutes on a phone show more nakedness than our grandfathers saw in a lifetime, and that shapes mind and morals.

outline.heading: Women valued for looks; marriage once came easily
outline.gist: Unveiling made a woman's worth her appearance; in earlier times the 'iddah was needed because suitors came at once, as with Asma bint Umays.

outline.heading: Why marriage is delayed today
outline.gist: Young people with far more money than past generations still do not marry; living amid normalised wrong has weakened us.

outline.heading: 'Bring us Allah's punishment' and Lut's prayer
outline.gist: No people is described in the Quran with as many ugly labels; any society that inverts right and wrong is headed for ruin unless it returns.

outline.heading: Lut harmed in his own home
outline.gist: Living among such a people splashes on you: his wife approved of them; he rejects the term derived from Lut's name for this act.

outline.heading: Expelled for being pure: the dominoes of values
outline.gist: When concepts flip, purity becomes a crime; this has reached Muslim lands, and our duty is to keep naming wrong as wrong.

outline.heading: Outro
